nameStory: The Blackberry Looper gets its name from its caterpillars' unusual way of moving and their favorite food. Like other 'looper' moths in the geometer family, the larvae arch their bodies into loops as they crawl, since they're missing some of the middle legs that other caterpillars have. The 'blackberry' part comes from their love of munching on blackberry fruits in the wild.
description: The Blackberry Looper is a small, delicate moth with a wingspan of just over half an inch to nearly an inch across. These pale green to whitish moths are members of the geometer family, known for their caterpillars that move in characteristic looping motions. Adults are active from spring through fall, with multiple generations each year. Despite their small size, they're surprisingly widespread across eastern North America.

idTips.label: Wing color and pattern
idTips.description: Pale green to whitish wings with subtle markings that can appear almost translucent when fresh, giving them a delicate, ethereal appearance

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small wingspan of 14-23mm (roughly the size of a nickel), making them one of the more petite moths you'll encounter

idTips.label: Body build
idTips.description: Slender, lightweight body that feels almost papery if gently handled, typical of the geometer moth family

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttering flight that appears almost bouncing or erratic, especially around lights at night

idTips.label: Wing position at rest
idTips.description: Wings held horizontally when at rest, creating a triangular silhouette rather than the tent-like shape of many other small moths

habitat: Look for Blackberry Looper Moths in areas where their favorite plants grow - woodland edges, old fields, and gardens with blackberry bushes, asters, goldenrod, and other composite flowers. They're particularly common in disturbed habitats like abandoned lots, forest clearings, and suburban areas where weedy flowers and berry bushes thrive. You'll often find them near outdoor lights at night, drawn in from nearby meadows and woodland borders.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in May in New England, with the first generation appearing as wildflowers start blooming. Look for them around early spring flowers and emerging blackberry canes.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple overlapping generations. Adults are most commonly seen at lights, while larvae feed on blackberry fruits and the petals of summer flowers like black-eyed Susans and asters.
seasonality.fall: Final generation appears through September, taking advantage of late-blooming goldenrod and fall asters. Adults become less common as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; the species overwinters in an inactive stage, likely as pupae or eggs, waiting for spring warmth to resume their life cycle.

funFact: While most moth caterpillars chew on leaves, Blackberry Looper larvae have a sweet tooth - they prefer to feast on flower petals and juicy blackberries, making them one of the few 'dessert specialist' moths in New England!
confusionNotes: Blackberry Loopers can be confused with other small, pale green moths, but their horizontal wing position at rest and association with berry patches and composite flowers helps distinguish them. Remember: if it's tiny, pale, and hanging around your blackberry bushes or wildflower garden, it's likely your looper.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'geometer' comes from Greek meaning 'earth measurer,' referring to how the caterpillars appear to be measuring the ground as they loop along. This family includes the familiar 'inchworms' that many people remember from childhood.
compareHints: Since this is the only Chlorochlamys species in our region, compare it to other small geometer moths by looking for the pale green to whitish coloration and relatively plain wing pattern. Most other small geometers in New England have more distinct markings, darker colors, or different wing shapes, making the Blackberry Looper's subtle, translucent appearance fairly distinctive once you know what to look for.
